## Function Disassemble

disassemble(code: bytes) -> list of (pc, op, arg) tuples, one per instruction, in code order: pc is the byte offset, op the opcode byte (int), arg the immediate bytes of PUSH1..PUSH32 (0x60..0x7f, n = op - 0x5f bytes) and b"" for every other opcode.

Behaviour: Every byte that is not a PUSH immediate is an instruction, including undefined opcodes (no name table, no validation). A PUSH whose immediate runs past the end of the code takes the bytes that are there (a shorter arg) and ends the list; nothing raises. Empty code gives []. PUSH0 (0x5f) has no immediate.

- reads: Runtime Code
- produces: Instruction

## Function Flag Risk

risk_flags(code: bytes) -> {"selfdestruct": bool, "mutable_delegatecall": bool}: two per-code security flags read from the runtime bytecode alone -- no source, no data-flow, no control-flow graph.

Behaviour: Both flags are read from the disassembly of the body from strip_metadata, so a 0xFF or 0xF4 byte inside a PUSH immediate or inside the metadata trailer never counts. selfdestruct is True when an opcode SELFDESTRUCT (0xFF) appears in that body: it marks the opcode present as an executable instruction, not a proof that some path reaches it (there is no CFG here, only disassembly). mutable_delegatecall is True when three conditions hold together: an opcode DELEGATECALL (0xF4) appears in the body, detect_proxy(code) is not "eip1167" (an EIP-1167 clone bakes its implementation address into the code and is excluded, however it is reached), and an opcode SLOAD (0x54) appears in the body -- the cheap syntactic stand-in, since data-flow is out of scope, for an implementation address that comes from storage rather than hardcoded. Order and position of the opcodes do not matter, only their presence. Never raises on empty or garbage bytes: risk_flags(b"") is both False.

## Function Spearman Matrix

spearman(rows) -> {"features": [...], "n": int, "matrix": [[...]]}, the rank correlation of the six numeric features of a code over every code of the base. The features, in this fixed order: bytecode_size, opcode_count, selector_count, address_count, l1_family_size, is_proxy.

Behaviour: bytecode_size is the fingerprint size, opcode_count is len(disassemble(code)), selector_count is the length of the selector list, address_count is len(addresses_of(code_id)), l1_family_size is the number of distinct code_id sharing this code's skeleton_hash counted over every code of the base, proxies included -- which is not the L1 cluster of Build Clusters, where proxies are excluded -- and is_proxy is 1 or 0. Ties are ranked by their average rank and the coefficient is then Pearson's on those ranks; the shortcut 1 - 6*sum(d^2)/(n*(n^2-1)) is wrong here and forbidden, because the base is full of ties (on one block 117 of 130 codes share one address_count). The matrix is square in the feature order, symmetric, with 1.0 on the diagonal. A feature with zero variance -- every value equal, as is_proxy on a base with no proxy -- gives null in every cell of its row and column, the diagonal included, and never a zero and never an exception. Fewer than two codes gives null everywhere. Standard library only: no numpy, no statistics beyond what is written here.

## Function Render Report

build_report(store, prefix, charts=None) -> (html_path, json_path) writes prefix + ".html" and prefix + ".json" and returns their paths. render_html(data, svgs) -> str builds the page from collected data and a mapping of chart name to SVG text. Two runs on the same store in the same environment give byte-identical html and json. The charts mapping has exactly the keys cluster_sizes, top_clusters, code_sizes, selector_counts and spearman; an absent or extra key is an error, not a silently missing picture.
